extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO in trademark matters (including U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing competent, ethical, and procedurally correct practice before the USPTO in trademark matters, including signature rules, client communications, supervision of non-practitioners, and disciplinary/compliance obligations. The document details violations, remedial steps, probation requirements, and reinstatement conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (requirement for U.S.-licensed attorney for foreign-domiciled applicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants or registrants must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.11; Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants and Registrants, 84 Fed. Reg. 31498 (July 2, 2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives: instill public confidence that registrations issued to foreign applicants are not subject to invalidation (e.g., improper signatures); increase compliance, improve accuracy of submissions, and safeguard integrity of the trademark register. Practitioners are expected to know and follow this rule (TMEP §601 and related materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature rules — personal entry requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory and a person electronically signing through TEAS must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a) and (c), and 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP and regulations require that the named signatory personally enter the electronic signature either directly on the filing system's form or in the emailed form. Failure to personally enter the signature violates the rule and may jeopardize application/registration validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on delegating signature or entering another's name
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may not delegate their authority to sign, and no person may sign or enter the name of another. Typing or otherwise entering the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person. See In re Zhang, TMEP §611.01(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document-signing software cannot be used to create or generate the electronic signature of the named signatory. Paralegals, legal assistants, secretaries, or foreign referral sources may not enter the attorney's or client's signature on trademark filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improperly executed signature renders submission unreliable and may jeopardize registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark submission signed by a person other than the named signatory is improperly executed and cannot be relied upon to support registration; a signature that does not meet the "personally signed" or "personally entered" requirements may jeopardize the validity of an application or registration. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(d) and § 2.193(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signature failures are substantive (not merely technical) and have precedential sanctions (e.g., In re Ste/core Management Services LLC). Improper signatures have led to cancellations and disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations under penalty of perjury and criminal exposure for false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications contain declarations signed under penalty of perjury; false or fraudulent statements are subject to punishment under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signatories make specific representations (use in commerce, intent to use) that USPTO relies upon; allowing others to sign such declarations can constitute violations of professional conduct and criminal statutes. See In re Hao and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on submitting false, fraudulent, or misleading information (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1) & (b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Submitting a document that includes false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information or representations violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1)." This includes false or misleading domicile information, attorney information, signatory information, applicant information, or claims of use (or intent to use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also violates §11.18(b)(2) when documents are submitted without reasonable inquiry into factual basis, evidentiary support, or in an effort to circumvent USPTO rules. Examples include fabricated deadlines, fake registration certificates, or false fee quotes described in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must provide competent representation to a client. Violations include not knowing or following the USPTO signature rules, presenting impermissibly signed documents, and not knowing that informed consent is required before accepting third-party payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes familiarity with USPTO signature and certification rules, the U.S. Counsel Rule, and TMEP provisions. Lack of practical trademark experience is not an excuse for failing to meet competence obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence in representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with reasonable diligence in representing a client. Presenting documents to the USPTO that were signed in violation of the trademark signature rules constitutes failure to act with reasonable diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes appropriate supervision of filings and timely communications with clients about problems affecting their filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication, consultation, and informed consent obligations (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must inform the client of decisions or circumstances requiring the client's informed consent and consult with the client about means to accomplish the client's objectives; must explain matters reasonably necessary to permit informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to inform Brand Mark Protect-referred clients of the attorney-client relationship, not obtaining informed consent to accept third-party payment, failing to communicate about improper signatures, and not timely informing clients about fraudulent schemes were cited as violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent to accept third-party payment (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must obtain informed consent from the client prior to accepting compensation for representing the client from someone other than the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting payment from a referring third party (e.g., Brand Mark Protect) without the client's informed consent violates this rule and is a basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision and responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must fulfill responsibilities for non-practitioner assistants; allowing, ordering, or facilitating non-practitioner assistants to present documents to the USPTO that are signed in violation of signature rules violates 11.503.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure non-attorney staff and foreign referral sources do not enter signatures or otherwise circumvent filing requirements; adequate supervision and systems are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving misrepresentation is prohibited. Examples include allowing or facilitating presentation of impermissibly signed trademark documents to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct can support disciplinary actions and is considered an aggravating factor in sanction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the federal trademark registration process (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that undermines the integrity of the federal trademark registration process (e.g., presenting impermissibly signed documents, failing to follow signature rules) violates § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO treats signature noncompliance as substantively harmful to the register and subject to discipline, not merely technical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry / evidentiary support for factual assertions (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must undertake a reasonable inquiry into factual bases for averments in trademark documents and have evidentiary support for assertions; submitting documents without reasonable inquiry may violate § 11.18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule applies to domicile, use claims, signatory information, and other facts. Circumventing rules or submitting documents without inquiry can be an improper purpose under §11.18(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to know and consult USPTO resources (TMEP, rulemaking, OED materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are reasonably expected to know applicable trademark prosecution rules, provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct implicated by representation, and potential disciplinary consequences. The USPTO provides guidance via the TMEP, rulemaking notices, and OED FOIA materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific references: TMEP §611.01 (signature rules), TMEP §601 (U.S. Counsel Rule), Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney final rule, and OED FOIA reading room. Practitioners should consult these resources as part of competent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and disciplinary consequences for violations (suspension, probation, additional suspension on noncompliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the signature rules, supervision, communication, and related professional-conduct rules can result in sanctions including suspension from practice, probation, orders to show cause, and further suspension for probation violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order describes a four-month suspension, limited recognition period, probation with conditions, and the possibility of up to an additional twelve months suspension for probation violations. Prior disciplinary decisions are cited as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and procedures under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 during suspension/limited recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: During suspension, the practitioner must comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 (including limited recognition for a short period to conclude client matters) and provide specific notifications to clients (and, for foreign clients, in the client's native language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements include how to send the Final Order/notice, acceptable email addresses to use (client email that practitioner reasonably believes the client can access), and procedures if using a referring foreign entity to forward notices (reasonable measures required and affidavit requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement prerequisites (education, review, CLE)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement, the practitioner must provide sworn declarations that she: (1) enrolled in, attended, and completed each of the eight modules of USPTO's Trademark Basics Boot Camp; (2) thoroughly reviewed all provisions of the TMEP including signature requirements; and (3) successfully completed two (2) hours of CLE in ethics/professional responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/statements must comply with 28 U.S.C. § 1746. These are mandatory remedial steps tied to reinstatement eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and reporting obligations during probation (bi-weekly searches and bimonthly reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation, the respondent must: (k) at least bi-weekly, search the USPTO online trademark search system for applications identifying her as attorney of record using a specified search phrase and promptly inform Trademark Policy of any trademark document identifying her as attorney of record that was filed without her knowledge or consent; and (l) at least every two months, submit a written report to OED stating completion of the bi-weekly searches and either that no unauthorized filings were found or provide copies of correspondence notifying Trademark Policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search phrase format provided: AT: firstname AND AT: lastname AND FD: [YYYYMMDD TO YYYYMMDD]. Reports and prompt notifications must be submitted to the Office of Trademark Examination Policy and OED as specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account management and sponsorship risks (disabling accounts, dissociation from Customer Numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon expiration of limited recognition the USPTO may disable or suspend any USPTO.gov accounts registered to the respondent; respondent's name shall be dissociated from any Customer Number(s) and USPTO verified Electronic System account(s), and the respondent shall not apply for, obtain, nor have her name added to a Customer Number or verified account until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who sponsor foreign agents or create sponsored accounts must be mindful that sponsoring or not supervising such accounts may violate trademark rules. The USPTO advises identity verification and frequent searches to detect unauthorized filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with USPTO inquiries into third-party entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall cooperate fully with the USPTO in any present or future inquiry into any third-party entities or persons with whom the practitioner worked or was solicited to work in connection with patent or trademark documents submitted to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation includes providing information about foreign referral sources, third-party contractors, and any evidence obtained during practice. Failure to cooperate can be an aggravating factor in enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification/contact-information obligations while on probation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation, respondent must notify the OED Director in writing within twenty-one (21) days of the date of the Final Order of a postal address, an email address, and a telephone number for correspondence; and must notify the OED Director of any change in those contact details within thirty (30) days of any change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the OED can correspond regarding Orders to Show Cause and other probation enforcement actions; failures may trigger expedited sanctions procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of available USPTO tools and reporting channels to detect and report unauthorized filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should regularly search the USPTO's online trademark search system to find applications naming them as attorney of record and, if unauthorized filings are found, promptly inform the USPTO via TMScams@uspto.gov or the Office of Trademark Examination Policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order gives a search string and recommends comparing search results to practitioner's own records to detect sponsored/unauthorized filings. This is presented as a best practice to protect the integrity of filings and the practitioner's clients.
